name: Non-Specific Low Back Pain
summary: Low back pain for which no specific serious structural cause is identified; management focuses on function, education and progressive activity.

looksLike: Pain with lifting, bending or prolonged positions
Possible buttock/thigh referral without clear neurological deficit
redFlags: New urinary retention/incontinence, saddle sensory loss or bilateral progressive weakness
Fever, immunosuppression, cancer history or unexplained weight loss
Significant trauma, fracture risk or prolonged steroid use
firstSteps: Explain the common non-specific nature and favourable prognosis for many episodes
Encourage continued daily activity and avoid bed rest
Use comfortable movement and short walking bouts
selfCare: Stay active within tolerable limits and avoid prolonged bed rest
Use a small, repeatable home program instead of many exercises
Gradually resume feared or avoided activities using patient-chosen functional goals
Agree how to adjust dose during a flare without defaulting to complete inactivity
Explain that pain intensity alone does not reliably show tissue damage; reassess if symptoms are new, progressive or inconsistent with the expected pattern

assess: Functional guarding or reduced activity tolerance
Neurological screen typically normal in uncomplicated cases
Pain behavior, onset, 24-hour pattern and functional limitations
Neurological screen and radicular symptoms when indicated
Screen for cauda equina symptoms, progressive neurological deficit, significant trauma/fracture risk, systemic illness and other serious pathology indicators
Repeated movements and directional preference when relevant; do not assume one preferred direction applies to every patient
Hip mobility and lower-limb strength where findings are relevant to the functional problem
Sleep, fear, work demands and psychosocial risk factors; discuss sensitive topics respectfully and collaboratively

tests.name: Neurological Screen of Lower Limbs
tests.purpose: Check myotomes, dermatomes and reflexes where leg symptoms or neurological concern are present.
tests.positive: Reproducible myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory change or reflex asymmetry.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Explain the common non-specific nature and favourable prognosis for many episodes
Encourage continued daily activity and avoid bed rest
Use comfortable movement and short walking bouts
Agree functional goals and address fear/avoidance
dose: Comfortable lumbar/hip movement: 5–10 reps, several times/day
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress trunk, hip and lower-limb strength according to deficits and goals
Use graded lifting, bending and aerobic conditioning
Individualise exercise rather than prescribe one supposedly corrective movement
dose: Trunk/hip strengthening: 2–4 sets of 6–15 reps, 2–3 days/week
Aerobic activity: build toward regular weekly activity
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Restore heavier lifting, work, caregiving or sport demands
Build capacity and confidence through progressive exposure
Create a sustainable activity and recurrence-management plan
dose: Task-specific lifting: 2–4 sets, gradually increasing load and range
Progress weekly volume based on function and 24-hour response
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Daily activities and work tasks resumed or modified safely

logic: First exclude serious spinal pathology and major neurological compromise.
Classify what mainly limits the patient: high irritability, movement fear, directional preference, deconditioning, load intolerance or persistent pain complexity.
Avoid over-medicalizing normal age-related imaging findings. Treatment should be driven by function and response, not MRI wording alone.
structures: Lumbar and lumbosacral tissues may contribute; routine clinical examination cannot reliably identify one pain-generating structure.
mechanism: Multifactorial interaction of loading, physical capacity, sleep, stress, health and contextual factors
May occur with lifting, prolonged positions or without a clear trigger
classification: Acute, subacute or persistent by duration
With or without referred leg pain; distinguish radicular features and red flags
investigations: Do not routinely image uncomplicated low back pain.
Urgent assessment and MRI pathway for suspected cauda equina or serious neurological compromise; investigate other red flags appropriately.
manual: Spinal or hip manual therapy may be offered as an adjunct for short-term relief in selected patients.
Pair manual therapy with exercise and self-management; do not claim to reposition vertebrae or correct a presumed lesion.
Lumbar or thoracic mobilization when it improves a comparable sign
Soft-tissue treatment for short-term symptom relief
Manipulation only when screened and clinically appropriate
Lumbar or thoracic mobilization: 30–60 seconds × 2–4 bouts when a comparable sign improves.
Soft-tissue work may help short-term pain or movement comfort but should be followed by active movement.
Manipulation may provide short-term benefit in selected patients after screening and consent, but it is not required for recovery.
modalities: Heat may be used for temporary symptom relief if helpful.
Avoid routine traction, passive electrotherapy or prolonged rest as core treatment.
Heat can be considered for short-term comfort
TENS may help selected patients temporarily
Routine passive electrotherapy should not displace active care
Heat: 10–20 minutes for short-term comfort if useful.
TENS can be trialed for temporary analgesia.
Avoid making traction, ultrasound or passive electrotherapy the central plan in routine non-specific low back pain.
dosing: Walking: start from the amount tolerated without a major flare and build by 5–10% as tolerated.
Directional-preference movement when clearly helpful: commonly 5–10 repetitions, several times/day.
Bridge, squat, hip hinge, row/carry or trunk exercises: 2–3 sets × 6–15 repetitions depending on tolerance.
For persistent pain, build general strength and aerobic capacity rather than endlessly searching for one 'weak core muscle'.
progression: Progress volume before intensity in deconditioned patients
Add loaded hinge, squat, carry and task-specific work as confidence improves
Increase one major variable at a time (load, repetitions, range, speed or task complexity)
Track function alongside pain using a patient-specific task or validated outcome measure
Reassess if function deteriorates, neurological signs progress or improvement does not follow the expected course
Progress from comfortable movement to loaded bending, squat, carry and lift.
Increase one variable at a time: range, load, repetitions or speed.
Use functional confidence and recovery after activity as progression markers.
mistakes: Overemphasis on posture, alignment or a single painful tissue
Ignoring psychosocial barriers or neurological changes
Telling the patient the back is 'out of place'.
Giving a complicated core program before restoring basic activity.
pearls: Use a biopsychosocial formulation without implying symptoms are imaginary.
Re-screen if new bladder, saddle, systemic or progressive neurological symptoms develop.
education: Explain that most non-specific low back pain improves with activity and graded loading.
Encourage normal movement and gradual return to meaningful tasks.
Explain red flags clearly without frightening the patient.
escalation: Immediate referral for cauda equina or severe neurological signs
Further medical review for persistent atypical or systemic symptoms

tests.name: Neurological Screen of Lower Limbs
tests.purpose: Check myotomes, dermatomes and reflexes where leg symptoms or neurological concern are present.
tests.positive: Reproducible myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory change or reflex asymmetry.
tests.patientPosition: Supine or seated; compare both sides and document each component.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: A deficit requires correlation with history and consideration of nerve-root or other neurological pathology.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
